title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
text:
On September 16, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised its federal-funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. Short-term benchmark rates adjusted immediately, but homebuyers do not borrow overnight: they usually finance a purchase for 15 or 30 years. This post asks a practical question:
The answer matters because buyers often shop by listing price when the binding constraint is actually monthly cash flow. I combine scraped policy, mortgage, and housing-market information with standard mortgage mathematics to translate an observed weekly rate difference into household-level dollar amounts.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Hidden Engines of Linear Dynamics
text:
Most relationships that economists put on a computer are, at their core, linear: regressions, vector autoregressions (VARs), Markov transition matrices, state-space models, and even the local approximations used to solve dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models. Every one of these tools repeatedly multiplies vectors by matrices.
A natural question follows:

When we multiply by the same matrix over and over, what happens in the long run — and why?

The complete answer is given by two objects that live inside the matrix itself: its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This post explains what they are, how to compute them by hand and in R, and why they do so much of the heavy lifting in economics — from the long-run unemployment rate to whether an estimated macro model is even stable.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Hidden Engines of Linear Dynamics
text:
2.1 Finding them: the characteristic equation
Moving \(\lambda\mathbf{v}\) to the left and inserting the identity matrix \(\mathbf{I}\) gives
\[
(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}.
\]
A non-zero solution \(\mathbf{v}\) exists exactly when the matrix \((\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\) is singular, i.e. its determinant is zero:
\[
\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = 0.
\]
This is the characteristic equation. It produces a polynomial in \(\lambda\) whose \(n\) roots are the eigenvalues; substituting each root back into \((\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\) gives the eigenvectors.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Hidden Engines of Linear Dynamics
text:
2.2 A worked 2 × 2 example
Take the symmetric matrix
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The characteristic equation is
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix} 2-\lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{pmatrix}
= (2-\lambda)^2 - 1
= \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3
= (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 3) = 0,
\]
so the eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1 = 3\) and \(\lambda_2 = 1\). The eigenvectors (defined only up to scale, so conventionally normalized to unit length) are
\[
\lambda_1 = 3: \quad \mathbf{v}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\lambda_2 = 1: \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Quick check: along the \(45^\circ\) direction, \(\mathbf{A}(1,1)' = (3,3)' = 3(1,1)'\), so the matrix stretches that direction threefold; along \((1,-1)'\) it leaves the vector exactly unchanged.

section: From the Fed to the front door

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
text:
The first pass-through was immediate
The H.15 table shows the effective federal-funds rate moving from 3.63% on September 16 to 3.88% on September 17. The bank prime rate simultaneously moved from 6.75% to 7.00%. Freddie Mac’s national average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose from 6.76% on September 10 to 6.95% on September 17—a 19-basis-point weekly increase. PMMS reflects thousands of conforming purchase-loan applications, so it is more informative than a single advertised quote.


Show the reproducible R code
p1 <- pmms |>
  filter(date >= ymd("2026-01-01"), date <= ymd("2026-09-17")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, mortgage_30y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#24496e") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ymd("2026-09-16"), linetype = "dashed", color = "#b24c3d") +
  geom_point(
    data = analysis_rates,
    size = 3,
    color = "#b24c3d"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "The 30-year mortgage rate climbed to 6.95%",
    subtitle = "Weekly national average, 2026 through September 17",
    x = NULL,
    y = "30-year fixed mortgage rate"
  )

p1
ggsave(here("figures", "mortgage-rate-trend.png"), p1, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)








Figure 1: Mortgage rates were already repricing before the September FOMC meeting. The highlighted points define the before-and-after affordability comparison. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS; author’s calculations.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Translating rates into a household budget
text:
Translating rates into a household budget
For principal \(L\), monthly rate \(r\), and \(N=360\) payments, monthly principal and interest are
\[
M=L\frac{r(1+r)^N}{(1+r)^N-1}.
\]
Using the Census Bureau’s July 2026 median new-home price of $393,800 and a 20% down payment, the observed weekly mortgage-rate increase raises monthly principal and interest from $2,045 to $2,085. That is $480 more per year, before property tax, insurance, maintenance, or HOA fees.


Show the reproducible R code
payment_grid <- crossing(
  mortgage_rate = seq(0.04, 0.08, by = 0.0005),
  loan = c(300000, 400000, 500000)
) |>
  mutate(monthly_payment = mortgage_payment(loan, mortgage_rate))

p2 <- ggplot(payment_grid, aes(mortgage_rate, monthly_payment, color = factor(loan))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(rate_before, rate_after), linetype = c("dotted", "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#3f7d5c", "#c17b31", "#8d4773"),
    labels = dollar(c(300000, 400000, 500000))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Small rate changes compound over 360 payments",
    subtitle = "Monthly principal and interest by loan size",
    x = "Mortgage rate",
    y = "Monthly payment",
    color = "Loan amount"
  )

p2
ggsave(here("figures", "payment-curves.png"), p2, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)








Figure 2: A higher rate raises the payment on the same loan. Calculations assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and show principal and interest only.





The reverse calculation is more useful for buyers. Holding the payment budget fixed,
\[
L_{max}=M\frac{1-(1+r)^{-N}}{r},
\]
so a higher rate reduces the loan a household can support.


Show the reproducible R code
budget_results <- crossing(
  monthly_budget = c(2000, 2500, 3000),
  period = factor(c("Before: 6.76%", "After: 6.95%"), levels = c("Before: 6.76%", "After: 6.95%"))
) |>
  mutate(
    rate = if_else(period == "Before: 6.76%", rate_before, rate_after),
    max_home_price = max_loan(monthly_budget, rate) / 0.80
  )

p3 <- ggplot(budget_results, aes(factor(monthly_budget), max_home_price, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = dollar(max_home_price, accuracy = 1000)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#7396b8", "#c65d45")) +
  labs(
    title = "The rate increase reduced purchasing power",
    subtitle = "Maximum home price supported by a fixed monthly budget",
    x = "Monthly principal-and-interest budget",
    y = "Maximum home price",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p3
ggsave(here("figures", "buying-power.png"), p3, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)








Figure 3: At a fixed monthly budget, a higher mortgage rate reduces the maximum affordable home price. Assumptions: 30-year term, 20% down, principal and interest only.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
text:
Takeaway: budget first, price second
The latest hike matters to buyers because higher financing costs reduce purchasing power even if house prices do not change. Yet the 19-basis-point weekly mortgage move is not a causal estimate of the Fed announcement: markets anticipated the meeting, and long-term rates and mortgage spreads moved at the same time.
The actionable response is therefore not to predict the next FOMC decision. Buyers should set a payment ceiling first, include taxes and insurance, and stress-test the budget at rates 50–100 basis points above today’s quote. Refinancing may become possible later, but it should not be required for the purchase to remain affordable. The central lesson is simple: the relevant price of a house is not its listing price alone; it is the cash-flow commitment created jointly by the price and the financing rate.

section: Research design: from websites to a decision
text:
Research design: from websites to a decision
The analysis follows a transparent pipeline:

Collect: scrape four public webpages with rvest and cache one dated HTML copy of each page.
Clean: convert table headings into dates, percentage strings into decimals, and price text into a numeric dollar value.
Validate: require the policy and mortgage observations used in the comparison to be present and nonmissing.
Calculate: apply the fixed-rate mortgage annuity formula under explicit assumptions.
Decide: convert the estimates into budget and stress-testing recommendations for prospective buyers.


Sources and ethical access








Source
Scraped information
Role in the analysis




Federal Reserve FOMC statement
Announced target range
Confirms the policy event


Federal Reserve H.15 table
Effective federal-funds and bank prime rates
Documents daily short-rate adjustment


Freddie Mac PMMS archive
Weekly 30- and 15-year mortgage rates
Measures household financing conditions


Census New Residential Sales
July 2026 median new-home sales price
Defines a nationally scaled illustrative scenario



All four pages are public and require no login, CAPTCHA, paywall, or access workaround. The script makes at most one request per source when a cached file is absent, waits before requesting, identifies the academic user agent, and reuses local HTML thereafter. This both limits server load and fixes the source vintage for reproducibility.
Freddie Mac’s September 17 PMMS observation is not a clean post-announcement mortgage rate. The weekly survey summarizes applications received largely from the preceding Thursday through Wednesday, so this observation covers approximately September 10–16, while the FOMC announcement occurred at 2:00 p.m. on September 16. I therefore call it the FOMC-week PMMS rate, not the “after” rate. The comparison below is descriptive and does not identify the causal effect of the announcement.

The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Finding 1: the transmission was immediate, but not one-for-one
text:
Finding 1: the transmission was immediate, but not one-for-one
The effective federal-funds rate moved from 3.63% to 3.88%, while the bank prime rate moved from 6.75% to 7.00%. These short-term rates followed the 25-basis-point policy move closely.
The 30-year mortgage rate behaved differently. It rose from 6.76% on September 10 to 6.95% on September 17, a 19-basis-point weekly increase. Figure 1 also shows that mortgage rates had been rising before the announcement. That is economically sensible because mortgage rates reflect expected future short rates, long-term yields, and mortgage-backed-security risk:
\[
r_t^{mortgage}
\approx
y_t^{10Y}+\text{MBS spread}_t.
\]


Show the reproducible R code
english_month_breaks <- ymd(sprintf("2026-%02d-01", 1:9))

p1 <- pmms |>
  filter(date >= ymd("2026-01-01"), date <= ymd("2026-09-17")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, mortgage_30y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "#24496e") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = ymd("2026-09-16"),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#b24c3d",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(data = analysis_rates, size = 3.2, color = "#b24c3d") +
  geom_text(
    data = analysis_rates,
    aes(label = percent(mortgage_30y, accuracy = 0.01)),
    vjust = -0.9,
    color = "#8f382d",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = english_month_breaks,
    labels = month.abb[1:9],
    limits = ymd(c("2026-01-01", "2026-09-22")),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "The 30-year mortgage rate reached ",
      percent(rate_after, accuracy = 0.01)
    ),
    subtitle = "Weekly national average, January-September 2026",
    x = NULL,
    y = "30-year fixed mortgage rate"
  )

ggsave(
  file.path(figure_dir, "mortgage-rate-trend.png"),
  p1,

  height = 5,

Figure 1: Figure 1. Weekly U.S. 30-year fixed mortgage rate. The red points are the September 10 and 17 comparison observations; the dashed line marks the September 16 FOMC decision. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS; author’s calculations.





The figure documents timing, not causality. A 19-basis-point weekly change is not a causal estimate of the FOMC announcement because markets anticipated the meeting and other rate components moved simultaneously. A causal design would require a narrower high-frequency event window and market instruments observed around the exact announcement time.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Finding 2: a small rate change compounds over 360 payments
text:
Finding 2: a small rate change compounds over 360 payments
For loan principal \(L\), monthly rate \(r\), and \(N=360\) payments, monthly principal and interest equal
\[
M=L\frac{r(1+r)^N}{(1+r)^N-1}.
\]
This nonlinear annuity formula converts the observed mortgage-rate change into a household cash-flow effect.


Show the reproducible R code
loan_values <- c(300000, 400000, 500000)

payment_grid <- crossing(
  mortgage_rate = seq(0.04, 0.08, by = 0.0005),
  loan = loan_values
) |>
  mutate(monthly_payment = mortgage_payment(loan, mortgage_rate))

p2 <- ggplot(
  payment_grid,
  aes(mortgage_rate, monthly_payment, color = factor(loan))
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = rate_before,
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = rate_after,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    color = "#b24c3d"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = rate_before,
    y = max(payment_grid$monthly_payment) * 0.985,
    label = before_label,
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 1.3,
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = rate_after,
    y = max(payment_grid$monthly_payment) * 0.985,
    label = after_label,
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = -0.4,
    color = "#8f382d",
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#3f7d5c", "#c17b31", "#8d4773"),
    breaks = as.character(loan_values),
    labels = dollar(loan_values)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Small rate changes compound over 360 payments",
    subtitle = "Monthly principal and interest by loan size",
    x = "Mortgage rate",
    y = "Monthly payment",
    color = "Loan amount"
  )

p2
ggsave(
  file.path(figure_dir, "payment-curves.png"),
  p2,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300

Figure 2: Figure 2. Monthly principal and interest for a 30-year fixed mortgage. The dotted and dashed lines mark the observed before and after rates. Taxes, insurance, fees, and maintenance are excluded.





Using the scraped Census median new-home price of $393,800 and a 20% down payment implies a $315,040 mortgage. Monthly principal and interest rise from $2,045 to $2,085: an increase of $40 per month, or $480 per year. In percentage terms, the payment rises by 1.95% even though the mortgage rate rises by only 19 basis points.
Figure 2 also reveals scale exposure. The same rate increase adds more dollars to the payment on a larger loan because the rate applies to a larger principal. This is why highly leveraged buyers are more sensitive to monetary tightening.

title: The Hidden Cost of a Rate Hike
section: Finding 3: fixed-budget buyers lose purchasing power
text:
Finding 3: fixed-budget buyers lose purchasing power
The more decision-relevant calculation holds the monthly budget fixed and solves the annuity formula for the maximum loan:
\[
L_{max}=M\frac{1-(1+r)^{-N}}{r}.
\]
With a 20% down payment, maximum home price is \(L_{max}/0.80\).


Show the reproducible R code
period_levels <- c(before_label, after_label)

budget_results <- crossing(
  monthly_budget = c(2000, 2500, 3000),
  period = period_levels
) |>
  mutate(
    period = factor(period, levels = period_levels),
    rate = if_else(period == before_label, rate_before, rate_after),
    max_home_price = max_loan(monthly_budget, rate) / 0.80
  )

budget_summary <- budget_results |>
  select(monthly_budget, period, max_home_price) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = max_home_price) |>
  mutate(
    dollar_loss = .data[[after_label]] - .data[[before_label]],
    percent_loss = .data[[after_label]] / .data[[before_label]] - 1
  )




Show the reproducible R code
p3 <- ggplot(
  budget_results,
  aes(factor(monthly_budget), max_home_price, fill = period)
) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = dollar(max_home_price, accuracy = 1000)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    vjust = -0.35,
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = dollar_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#7396b8", "#c65d45"),
    breaks = period_levels
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Higher rates reduce homebuying power",
    subtitle = "Maximum price supported by the same monthly budget",
    x = "Monthly principal-and-interest budget",
    y = "Maximum home price",
    fill = NULL

  theme(legend.position = "top")

p3

  file.path(figure_dir, "buying-power.png"),

  width = 8,

title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
text:
Decision rule and stress test
The observed weekly difference is modest compared with the rate uncertainty a buyer may face between preapproval and closing. A practical decision rule is therefore to choose a home price that remains within the buyer’s all-in budget under a higher-rate scenario, not merely at today’s quoted rate.


Show the reproducible R code
stress_test <- tibble(
  Scenario = c(
    "Previous-week PMMS rate",
    "FOMC-week PMMS rate",
    "FOMC-week rate + 50 bp",
    "FOMC-week rate + 100 bp"
  ),
  mortgage_rate = c(
    rate_previous_week,
    rate_fomc_week,
    rate_fomc_week + 0.005,
    rate_fomc_week + 0.010
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    maximum_loan = max_loan(2500, mortgage_rate),
    maximum_home_price = maximum_loan / 0.80
  )

stress_test |>
  transmute(
    Scenario,
    `Mortgage rate` = percent(mortgage_rate, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Maximum loan` = dollar(maximum_loan, accuracy = 1),
    `Home price supported by assumed P&I budget` =

title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
section: What this analysis can and cannot establish
text:
What this analysis can and cannot establish
The evidence supports a cash-flow scenario, not a causal monetary-policy estimate. PMMS is a national weekly average, and the September 17 observation largely summarizes applications submitted before the September 16 announcement. An individual quote also depends on credit score, loan-to-value ratio, points, geography, and loan type. The Census input is the July 2026 national median for newly built single-family homes, not a September price and not the median for all U.S. housing transactions. Most importantly, comparing two weekly PMMS releases cannot isolate the surprise component of monetary policy from expectations or other news.
A deeper follow-up could merge daily Treasury yields and mortgage-backed-security spreads, separate expected policy from announcement surprises, and compare metro areas with different price levels. That extension would test whether a given rate shock has larger dollar effects in expensive markets and whether changing spreads amplify or absorb policy-rate movements.

title: The Hidden Cost of Higher Mortgage Rates
text:
Takeaway
The September episode contains two related but empirically distinct developments: the policy decision mechanically raised short-term benchmark rates, while the FOMC-week PMMS mortgage rate was also higher than the previous week’s reading. Applying that observed weekly difference to a standard amortization model shows how even a modestly higher mortgage rate can reduce the home price supported by a fixed principal-and-interest budget. For buyers, the relevant cost of a house is therefore not its listing price alone; it is the long-term cash-flow commitment jointly created by the price, down payment, and financing rate.

Finding 3: a fixed P&I budget supports a lower purchase price at a higher rate
The more decision-relevant calculation holds the monthly budget fixed and solves the annuity formula for the maximum loan:
\[

Research Design
The analysis follows a transparent pipeline:

Collect: scrape four public webpages with rvest and cache one dated HTML copy of each page.
Clean: convert table headings into dates, percentage strings into decimals, and price text into a numeric dollar value.
Validate: require the policy and mortgage observations used in the comparison to be present and nonmissing.
Calculate: apply the fixed-rate mortgage annuity formula under explicit assumptions.
Decide: convert the estimates into budget and stress-testing recommendations for prospective buyers.

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
text:
Data and analysis pipeline
The data do not arrive as a ready-made table of “mothers with toddlers versus fathers with toddlers.” The R code above asks the IPUMS API for the 2025 ASEC person-level extract (cps2025_03s) in CSV format. IPUMS sends a compressed CSV and an XML data dictionary (DDI). The first render downloads them to a private cache outside this website; later renders reuse a complete download. The extract request is saved there too, so an interrupted download can resume without asking IPUMS to build another extract.








IPUMS variable
What it supplies
How this article uses it




YEAR, AGE
Survey year and age
Confirm 2025; keep ages 25–54


SEX
CPS recorded sex
Compare groups labelled women and men


YNGCH
Age of youngest own child living in the household
Define the child-age groups


EMPSTAT
Employment and labor-force status
Build employment, participation, and unemployment measures


EDUC
Highest educational attainment
Separate bachelor’s degree or higher from below bachelor’s in the model


ASECWT
ASEC person weight
Estimate population rates and fit the weighted model


REPWTP1–REPWTP160
ASEC person replicate weights
Compute survey-based uncertainty, including error bars



The next code block creates four mutually exclusive groups: no resident minor own child, youngest own child 0–5, 6–12, or 13–17. It keeps adults ages 25–54 with a known employment status and positive person weight, excludes unknown education (EDUC = 999), and converts employment into a 0/1 indicator. Someone without a resident minor child may still be a parent. The code then computes weighted rates separately for each sex and child group.


Show the R code
# Step 5: recode child age, employment and controls; retain eligible adults.
# EMPSTAT general code 1 = employed; 2 = unemployed; 3 = not in labor force.
# YNGCH 99 = no identified own child living in the household.
# EDUC 999 = missing or unknown. EDUC 000 may also mean no schooling, so retain it.
cps <- cps_raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = factor(as.numeric(SEX), levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    child_group = dplyr::case_when(
      YNGCH == 99 | YNGCH >= 18 ~ "no_minor",
      YNGCH >= 0 & YNGCH <= 5 ~ "age0_5",
      YNGCH >= 6 & YNGCH <= 12 ~ "age6_12",
      YNGCH >= 13 & YNGCH <= 17 ~ "age13_17",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    child_group = factor(child_group,
                         levels = c("no_minor", "age0_5", "age6_12", "age13_17")),
    status = floor(as.numeric(EMPSTAT) / 10),
    employed = as.numeric(status == 1),
    labor_force = as.numeric(status %in% c(1, 2)),
    unemployed = as.numeric(status == 2),
    age_band = factor(dplyr::case_when(
      AGE <= 34 ~ "25–34", AGE <= 44 ~ "35–44", TRUE ~ "45–54"
    ), levels = c("25–34", "35–44", "45–54")),
    college = factor(ifelse(EDUC >= 111, "BA or higher", "Below BA"),
                     levels = c("Below BA", "BA or higher"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 54, !is.na(sex), !is.na(child_group),
                status %in% c(1, 2, 3), !is.na(EDUC), EDUC != 999,
                !is.na(ASECWT), ASECWT > 0)
if (!nrow(cps)) stop("No eligible records: inspect IPUMS variable codes.")
# Step 6: make the ASEC person-weighted survey design with all 160 replicates.
design <- srvyr::as_survey_rep(
  cps, weight = ASECWT, repweights = dplyr::matches("^REPWTP[0-9]+$"),
  type = "successive-difference", mse = TRUE
)
# Step 7: estimate eight group rates and their design-based confidence intervals.
rates <- design |>
  dplyr::group_by(sex, child_group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    employment = srvyr::survey_mean(employed, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    participation = srvyr::survey_mean(labor_force, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    unemployment = srvyr::survey_ratio(unemployed, labor_force,
                                        vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  as.data.frame()
readr::write_csv(rates, file.path(derived_dir, "weighted_rates.csv"))
pick_rate <- function(s, g, col = "employment") {
  row <- rates[rates$sex == s & rates$child_group == g, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(row) != 1L) stop("An expected group is missing: ", s, ", ", g)
  as.numeric(row[[col]])
}
e_w_young <- pick_rate("Women", "age0_5")
e_m_young <- pick_rate("Men", "age0_5")
e_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor")
e_m_none <- pick_rate("Men", "no_minor")
women_gap <- 100 * (e_w_young - e_w_none)
men_gap <- 100 * (e_m_young - e_m_none)
fmt_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
fmt_pp <- function(x) sprintf("%+.1f percentage points", x)


The API extract contained 142,125 person records; after the stated sample restrictions, 54,607 records enter the analysis. These are sample counts, not estimates of the population size. The employment rate is the weighted share working; participation is the weighted share working or looking for work; unemployment divides weighted job seekers by the weighted labor force. All three rates are stored in data/derived/weighted_rates.csv.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: 1. First, what do the employment rates say?
text:
1. First, what do the employment rates say?
The CPS interviews a sample, so a respondent does not necessarily represent the same number of people as another respondent. We calculate each group’s employment rate with the ASEC person weight, ASECWT, rather than counting sample records equally. The slim vertical lines in the figure show 95% confidence intervals calculated with the survey’s person replicate weights.


Show the R code
# Step 8: plot and save weighted employment rates and their intervals.
labels <- c(no_minor = "No resident minor child", age0_5 = "Youngest child 0–5",
            age6_12 = "Youngest child 6–12", age13_17 = "Youngest child 13–17")
palette <- c(Men = "#147d87", Women = "#db6b54")
theme_blog <- function() ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 plot.title.position = "plot", legend.position = "top",
                 plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", color = "#17304b"))
p1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(rates,
                      ggplot2::aes(x = child_group, y = 100 * employment,
                                   color = sex)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .5), size = 3) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = 100 * employment_low, ymax = 100 * employment_upp),
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .5), width = .15
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = labels) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = palette) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Employment across household stages",
                x = NULL, y = "Employed (%)", color = NULL) +
  theme_blog() +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "figure1_employment.png"), p1,
                width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 200)
p1








Figure 1: Weighted employment-to-population ratios for adults ages 25–54. Source: IPUMS CPS, 2025 ASEC. Error bars are 95% design-based confidence intervals.





Among adults with a youngest resident child ages 0–5, the weighted employment rate is 67.7% for women and 93.6% for men. Relative to adults with no resident minor child, the within-sex differences are -9.9 percentage points for women and +12.7 percentage points for men. These are descriptive comparisons: the household groups may differ in age, education, and circumstances we cannot measure here.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: 2. Not working is not always unemployment
text:
2. Not working is not always unemployment
An adult who is not working may be looking for work, or may be outside the labor force. That distinction changes the interpretation of the first chart. Participation is the share of everyone in the group who works or is seeking work. Unemployment is the share of labor-force members who are seeking work without a job. Notice that the two panels have different vertical scales and denominators; compare patterns within each panel.


Show the R code
# Step 9: plot and save labor-force participation and unemployment.
panels <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(rates, sex, child_group,
                   measure = "Labor-force participation", value = 100 * participation),
  dplyr::transmute(rates, sex, child_group,
                   measure = "Unemployment among the labor force", value = 100 * unemployment)
)
p2 <- ggplot2::ggplot(panels,
                      ggplot2::aes(x = child_group, y = value,
                                   color = sex, group = sex)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = labels) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = palette) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Not employed does not always mean unemployed",
                x = NULL, y = "Percent (panel-specific denominator)", color = NULL) +
  theme_blog() +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "figure2_labor_force.png"), p2,
                width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 200)
p2








Figure 2: Two complementary labor-market measures. Participation divides by all adults in a group; unemployment divides only by adults in its labor force. Source: IPUMS CPS, 2025 ASEC.







Show the R code
lf_w_young <- pick_rate("Women", "age0_5", "participation")
lf_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor", "participation")
u_w_young <- pick_rate("Women", "age0_5", "unemployment")
u_w_none <- pick_rate("Women", "no_minor", "unemployment")
participation_sentence <- if (lf_w_young < lf_w_none) {
  "is lower"
} else if (lf_w_young > lf_w_none) {
  "is higher"
} else {
  "is equal"
}


For women with a youngest resident child ages 0–5, participation is lower than among women with no resident minor child (69.8% versus 80.3%). The corresponding unemployment rates are 3.0% and 3.5%. These measures help locate the descriptive source of an employment-rate difference. They cannot tell us why a person is outside the labor force.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
section: 3. What if we compare similar ages and education?
text:
3. What if we compare similar ages and education?
The first chart compares real population groups, but those groups may have different age and education mixes. A survey-weighted linear probability model compares employment across child groups while accounting for age band and education, with a separate young-child contrast for women and men. Think of it as checking whether our first comparison changes when we make those two measured characteristics more alike. The result is still an association.


Show the R code
# Step 10: estimate adjusted within-sex gaps and their difference.
model <- survey::svyglm(
  employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college,
  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()
)
b <- stats::coef(model)
V <- stats::vcov(model)
ci_critical <- stats::qt(0.975, df = 159) # 160 replicates imply 159 design df.
men_term <- "child_groupage0_5"
interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"
stopifnot(all(c(men_term, interaction_term) %in% names(b)))
contrast <- function(label, terms) {
  cvec <- stats::setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  cvec[terms] <- 1
  estimate <- sum(cvec * b)
  se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(cvec) %*% V %*% cvec))
  data.frame(group = label, estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
             lower_pp = 100 * (estimate - ci_critical * se),
             upper_pp = 100 * (estimate + ci_critical * se), se_pp = 100 * se)
}
adjusted <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  contrast("Men", men_term),
  contrast("Women", c(men_term, interaction_term)),
  contrast("Women minus men", interaction_term)
)
readr::write_csv(adjusted, file.path(derived_dir, "adjusted_gaps.csv"))
capture.output(summary(model), file = file.path(derived_dir, "model_summary.txt"))
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = file.path(derived_dir, "session_info.txt"))
adj_w <- adjusted$estimate_pp[adjusted$group == "Women"]
adj_m <- adjusted$estimate_pp[adjusted$group == "Men"]
interaction <- adjusted[adjusted$group == "Women minus men", ]
uncertainty_phrase <- if (interaction$lower_pp <= 0 && interaction$upper_pp >= 0) {
  "includes zero, so this sample does not pin down the direction of that contrast"
} else {
  "does not include zero, indicating a detectable contrast under this survey design"
}




Show the R code
# Step 11: plot and save the model's within-sex contrasts.
p3 <- ggplot2::ggplot(dplyr::filter(adjusted, group != "Women minus men"),
                      ggplot2::aes(y = group, x = estimate_pp, color = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "#80909b") +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(xmin = lower_pp, xmax = upper_pp),
                         orientation = "y", width = .13) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = palette, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "The young-child association after adjustment",
                x = "Employment-rate difference (percentage points)", y = NULL) +
  theme_blog()
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(figure_dir, "figure3_adjusted_gaps.png"), p3,
                width = 9, height = 4.5, dpi = 200)
p3








Figure 3: Adjusted difference in employment rate: youngest resident child ages 0–5 minus no resident minor child, within sex. Points use an age- and education-adjusted survey-weighted model; bars are 95% design-based confidence intervals.





After adjustment, the young-child versus no-minor-child difference is -10.7 percentage points for women and +11.2 percentage points for men. The difference between these two contrasts is -21.9 percentage points. Its 95% interval, from -23.9 to -20.0 percentage points, does not include zero, indicating a detectable contrast under this survey design. This interval describes sampling uncertainty; unmeasured differences between households remain.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
text:
What should we take away?
The youngest child’s age and employment can be related in different ways for women and men. We have documented that relationship in population-weighted comparisons, checked whether participation and unemployment tell the same story, and tested how much the comparison changes after accounting for age and education. The strongest honest conclusion is about patterns among households, not what any particular child did to a parent’s career. A toddler may rearrange the morning schedule; these data alone cannot identify the counterfactual career path.






Reading the evidence carefully



The CPS variable SEX records survey categories labelled women and men here; it is not a measure of gender identity. YNGCH covers co-resident children identified by IPUMS family links. The model is descriptive and does not establish a causal effect of parenthood.

title: Tiny Shoes, Big Questions
text:
Methods and replication
For a group \(g\), its weighted employment rate is \(\hat p_g=\sum_{i\in g}w_i 1\{i\text{ employed}\}/\sum_{i\in g}w_i\), where \(w_i\) is ASECWT. The third chart fits a linear probability model with sex-by-child-group interactions, three age bands and two education groups. We use the 160 ASEC person replicate weights (REPWTP1–REPWTP160) for sampling uncertainty. Every number in the article is computed on render.

The code runs top to bottom: install/check packages → request or reuse the extract → read and clean records → define survey weights → calculate rates → draw three figures → estimate and interpret the model. The figures and aggregate CSVs are created on each render.
Register for IPUMS CPS and obtain an API key. The first render installs any missing R packages from CRAN; package installation may take a few minutes. title: The employment divide around young children

The survey and the comparison
The unit is a person, aged 25 to 54. IPUMS’s YNGCH identifies the youngest own child living in that person’s household; the definition includes biological, step and adopted children. The reference group has no own child under 18 living at home. It can include parents with adult children or children living elsewhere, so it should not be called a childless group.
The API request obtains the 2025 ASEC person extract (cps2025_03s) and its XML dictionary. The first run stores the person records in a private cache outside the website; subsequent runs reuse the download. We exclude missing employment or education responses and records with nonpositive person weights.

title: The employment divide around young children
section: The employment gap points in opposite directions
text:
The employment gap points in opposite directions

title: The employment divide around young children
section: What lies behind the employment rates?
text:
What lies behind the employment rates?
Employment is one of three possible states in this classification. An adult can also be unemployed and seeking work, or outside the labor force. The participation rate counts employed people and job seekers as a share of all adults in a group. The unemployment rate counts job seekers as a share of that group’s labor force. Their denominators differ, so the two panels below have separate scales.

title: The employment divide around young children
section: Does the contrast survive basic adjustment?
text:
Does the contrast survive basic adjustment?
The household groups need not have the same age or education mix. We fit a survey-weighted linear probability model for being employed, including recorded sex, child-age group, their interaction, age band and whether the person has a bachelor’s degree. In plain terms, the model asks whether the contrast remains when we compare people in the same broad age and education categories. The interaction asks whether the young-child contrast is different for women and men. This model cannot hold constant unobserved income, partnership, child care access or preferences.


Show R code
model <- survey::svyglm(
  employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college,
  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()
)
b <- stats::coef(model)
V <- stats::vcov(model)
ci_critical <- stats::qt(.975, df = 159) # 160 person replicates, 159 df.
men_term <- "child_groupage0_5"
interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"
stopifnot(all(c(men_term, interaction_term) %in% names(b)))
contrast <- function(label, terms) {
  cvec <- stats::setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  cvec[terms] <- 1
  estimate <- sum(cvec * b)
  se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(cvec) %*% V %*% cvec))
  data.frame(group = label, estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
             lower_pp = 100 * (estimate - ci_critical * se),
             upper_pp = 100 * (estimate + ci_critical * se), se_pp = 100 * se)
}
adjusted <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  contrast("Men", men_term),
  contrast("Women", c(men_term, interaction_term)),
  contrast("Women minus men", interaction_term)
)
readr::write_csv(adjusted, file.path(derived_dir, "adjusted_gaps.csv"))
capture.output(summary(model), file = file.path(derived_dir, "model_summary.txt"))
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = file.path(derived_dir, "session_info.txt"))
adj_w <- adjusted$estimate_pp[adjusted$group == "Women"]
adj_m <- adjusted$estimate_pp[adjusted$group == "Men"]
interaction <- adjusted[adjusted$group == "Women minus men", ]

  dplyr::mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("Men", "Women")),
                label = sprintf("%+.1f pp", estimate_pp))

    ggplot2::aes(x = estimate_pp, y = group, color = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "#7a8890", linewidth = .55) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(xmin = lower_pp, xmax = upper_pp),

The women’s contrast minus the men’s is -21.9 percentage points; its 95% interval runs from -23.9 to -20.0 percentage points. The interval excludes zero under the specified survey design. Adjustment changes the comparison’s composition on two measured dimensions; it does not turn the contrast into a causal effect of having a child.

title: The employment divide around young children
text:
The economic reading
The striking feature of these data is the opposite sign of the young-child comparison for women and men. For women, lower employment accompanies lower labor force participation, rather than higher unemployment among participants. For men, both employment and participation are higher in the young-child group than in the reference group. Broad age and education controls leave that contrast in place.
Several stories could produce these patterns: different division of paid and unpaid work, selection into parenthood, partnership and household income, or constraints around child care. The CPS snapshot cannot separate those mechanisms. The result is a well-measured description of who is working across household types, and a reason to ask better questions about the choices and constraints behind it.

title: The employment divide around young children
text:
Methods and reproducibility
The employment rate is the ASECWT-weighted share employed within each sex and child group. Participation is the weighted share employed or unemployed; unemployment is the weighted number unemployed divided by the weighted labor force. The code checks that employment equals participation multiplied by one minus unemployment (up to rounding). The model is a linear probability model with sex-by-child-group interactions. The 160 ASEC person replicate weights and the survey design supply standard errors and confidence intervals. SEX is the CPS recorded sex variable and does not measure gender identity.

# Step 5: recode child age, employment and controls; retain eligible adults.
# EMPSTAT general code 1 = employed; 2 = unemployed; 3 = not in labor force.
# YNGCH 99 = no identified own child living in the household.
# EDUC 999 = missing or unknown. EDUC 000 may also mean no schooling, so retain it.
cps <- cps_raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex = factor(as.numeric(SEX), levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    child_group = dplyr::case_when(
      YNGCH == 99 | YNGCH >= 18 ~ "no_minor",
      YNGCH >= 0 & YNGCH <= 5 ~ "age0_5",
      YNGCH >= 6 & YNGCH <= 12 ~ "age6_12",
      YNGCH >= 13 & YNGCH <= 17 ~ "age13_17",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    child_group = factor(child_group,
                         levels = c("no_minor", "age0_5", "age6_12", "age13_17")),
    status = floor(as.numeric(EMPSTAT) / 10),
    employed = as.numeric(status == 1),
    labor_force = as.numeric(status %in% c(1, 2)),
    unemployed = as.numeric(status == 2),
    age_band = factor(dplyr::case_when(
      AGE <= 34 ~ "25-34", AGE <= 44 ~ "35-44", TRUE ~ "45-54"
    ), levels = c("25-34", "35-44", "45-54")),
    college = factor(ifelse(EDUC >= 111, "BA or higher", "Below BA"),
                     levels = c("Below BA", "BA or higher"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 54, !is.na(sex), !is.na(child_group),
                status %in% c(1, 2, 3), !is.na(EDUC), EDUC != 999,
                !is.na(ASECWT), ASECWT > 0)
if (!nrow(cps)) stop("No eligible records: inspect IPUMS variable codes.")
# Audit the sample restriction. These are unweighted person records.

n_prime_age <- sum(!is.na(cps_raw$AGE) & cps_raw$AGE >= 25 & cps_raw$AGE <= 54)
n_analytic <- nrow(cps)
stopifnot(n_analytic <= n_prime_age, n_prime_age <= n_downloaded)
# Step 6: make the ASEC person-weighted survey design with all 160 replicates.

  cps, weight = ASECWT, repweights = dplyr::matches("^REPWTP[0-9]+$"),
  type = "successive-difference", mse = TRUE
)
# Step 7: estimate eight group rates and their design-based confidence intervals.

  dplyr::group_by(sex, child_group) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    employment = srvyr::survey_mean(employed, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    participation = srvyr::survey_mean(labor_force, vartype = "ci", na.rm = TRUE),
    unemployment = srvyr::survey_ratio(unemployed, labor_force,

stopifnot(max(abs(rates$employment - rates$participation *

section: Does age and education adjustment change the picture?
text:
Does age and education adjustment change the picture?
The groups differ in more than family circumstances. For a descriptive check, I estimate a survey-weighted linear probability model. The outcome is one if a person is employed and zero otherwise. Let \(F_i\) indicate a woman, \(C_{ig}\) indicate the youngest-child group \(g\) (relative to no minor child at home), \(A_i\) denote age-band indicators and \(B_i\) indicate a bachelor’s degree or higher. The estimated equation is
\[
\Pr(E_i=1 \mid F_i,C_i,A_i,B_i)
= \alpha + \beta F_i + \sum_g \gamma_g C_{ig}
+ \sum_g \delta_g(F_i C_{ig}) + \boldsymbol{\theta}' A_i + \lambda B_i.
\]
For the 0-to-5 group, \(\gamma_{0-5}\) is the adjusted difference for men; \(\gamma_{0-5}+\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference for women; and \(\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference between those two differences. The reference person is a man aged 25 to 34, without a bachelor’s degree and without an own minor child at home. Model coefficients are percentage-point changes when multiplied by 100, not percentage changes.

}

title: When Young Children Are at Home, Who Is at Work?
text:
Takeaway

A divide the data can reveal, but not explain

The survey reveals two distinct labor market patterns around young children: women in the 0-to-5 household group are less likely to be employed than women without a minor child at home, while men in the corresponding group are more likely to be employed. For women, participation rather than unemployment is the more informative margin. The difference survives broad age and education adjustment. It points to an important question for child care and work policy: what combination of care costs, household specialization, earnings and selection into parenthood lies behind it? This cross-sectional comparison cannot distinguish those mechanisms or support a causal claim.

section: Does the divide remain after adjustment?
text:
Does the divide remain after adjustment?
The groups differ in more than family circumstances. For a descriptive check, I estimate a survey-weighted linear probability model. The outcome is one if a person is employed and zero otherwise. Let \(F_i\) indicate a woman, \(C_{ig}\) indicate the youngest-child group \(g\) (relative to no minor child at home), \(A_i\) denote age-band indicators and \(B_i\) indicate a bachelor’s degree or higher. The estimated equation is
\[
\Pr(E_i=1 \mid F_i,C_i,A_i,B_i)
= \alpha + \beta F_i + \sum_g \gamma_g C_{ig}
+ \sum_g \delta_g(F_i C_{ig}) + \boldsymbol{\theta}' A_i + \lambda B_i.
\]
For the 0-to-5 group, \(\gamma_{0-5}\) is the adjusted difference for men; \(\gamma_{0-5}+\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference for women; and \(\delta_{0-5}\) is the difference between those two differences. The reference person is a man aged 25 to 34, without a bachelor’s degree and without an own minor child at home. Model coefficients are percentage-point changes when multiplied by 100, not percentage changes.


Show R code
model <- survey::svyglm(
  employed ~ sex * child_group + age_band + college,
  design = design, family = stats::gaussian()
)
b <- stats::coef(model)
V <- stats::vcov(model)
ci_critical <- stats::qt(.975, df = 159) # 160 person replicates, 159 design df.
men_term <- "child_groupage0_5"
interaction_term <- "sexWomen:child_groupage0_5"
stopifnot(all(c(men_term, interaction_term) %in% names(b)))
contrast <- function(label, terms) {
  cvec <- stats::setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
  cvec[terms] <- 1
  estimate <- sum(cvec * b)
  se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(cvec) %*% V %*% cvec))
  data.frame(group = label, estimate_pp = 100 * estimate,
             lower_pp = 100 * (estimate - ci_critical * se),
             upper_pp = 100 * (estimate + ci_critical * se), se_pp = 100 * se)
}
adjusted <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  contrast("Men", men_term),
  contrast("Women", c(men_term, interaction_term)),
  contrast("Women minus men", interaction_term)
)

capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = file.path(derived_dir, "session_info.txt"))

adj_m <- adjusted$estimate_pp[adjusted$group == "Men"]
